I was still in a phase where I thoroughly enjoyed make-believe games, so I didn't join them very often, but they were there from year 5 onwards. </p><p>The event in question happened on one of the days in year 6 that I was spending time with the gynmastics girls instead of my usual make-believe friends. We had all gathered in a little huddle in the playground when one of us had started talking specifically about another girl in our class - April. Suddenly, with an viciousness I didn't really realise people had at the age of 11, the entire group of girls was insulting and laughing at April behind her back. Most shockingly, her supposed 'best friend' Roxanne was leading the charge. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. So I joined in. I remember saying exactly one thing that mostly boiled down to: \"I don't like her singing voice in assemblies\" (we went to a Church of England school - hymns were daily and VERY annoying). </p><p>At the end of the break we all went our separate ways back to class, and I felt at least a little comforted by the fact that no one seemed to be bringing up our little bitch-fest after it had concluded.</p><p>Until, terrifyingly, all of our group were called to the front of the class the next day.</p><p>We huddled at the front of the room whilst the rest of the class worked on their class work, and Mrs Chadbourne stared us all down, then brought April over too. I was still in a phase where I thoroughly enjoyed make-believe games, so I didn't join them very often, but they were there from year 5 onwards. </p><p>The event in question happened on one of the days in year 6 that I was spending time with the gynmastics girls instead of my usual make-believe friends. We had all gathered in a little huddle in the playground when one of us had started talking specifically about another girl in our class - April. Suddenly, with an viciousness I didn't really realise people had at the age of 11, the entire group of girls was insulting and laughing at April behind her back. Most shockingly, her supposed 'best friend' Roxanne was leading the charge. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. So I joined in. I remember saying exactly one thing that mostly boiled down to: \"I don't like her singing voice in assemblies\" (we went to a Church of England school - hymns were daily and VERY annoying). </p><p>At the end of the break we all went our separate ways back to class, and I felt at least a little comforted by the fact that no one seemed to be bringing up our little bitch-fest after it had concluded.</p><p>Until, terrifyingly, all of our group were called to the front of the class the next day.</p><p>We huddled at the front of the room whilst the rest of the class worked on their class work, and Mrs Chadbourne stared us all down, then brought April over too. My face - and stomach - dropped. I remember knowing instantly that we had been rumbled and feeling SO awful about it. Mrs Chadbourne gave some speech about us needing to look after other peoples feelings more, and whilst everyone else seemed to be staring daggers at Roxanne (who had switched up on us and had been the person to rat us out), I was looking at April's devastated face. I burst out crying, apologising manically, and she started crying too saying she forgave me and we both hugged. Mrs Chadbourne commended me on being the first to apologise and sentenced all of us to a lunchtime detention - unheard of in a primary school, seriously who would do that?</p><p>Even though April had forgiven me, I remember spending a really long time after feeling awful every time I looked at her. Suddenly, with an viciousness I didn't really realise people had at the age of 11, the entire group of girls was insulting and laughing at April behind her back. Most shockingly, her supposed 'best friend' Roxanne was leading the charge. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. I was still in a phase where I thoroughly enjoyed make-believe games, so I didn't join them very often, but they were there from year 5 onwards. </p><p>The event in question happened on one of the days in year 6 that I was spending time with the gynmastics girls instead of my usual make-believe friends. We had all gathered in a little huddle in the playground when one of us had started talking specifically about another girl in our class - April. Suddenly, with an viciousness I didn't really realise people had at the age of 11, the entire group of girls was insulting and laughing at April behind her back. Most shockingly, her supposed 'best friend' Roxanne was leading the charge. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. So I joined in. I remember saying exactly one thing that mostly boiled down to: \"I don't like her singing voice in assemblies\" (we went to a Church of England school - hymns were daily and VERY annoying). </p><p>At the end of the break we all went our separate ways back to class, and I felt at least a little comforted by the fact that no one seemed to be bringing up our little bitch-fest after it had concluded.</p><p>Until, terrifyingly, all of our group were called to the front of the class the next day.</p><p>We huddled at the front of the room whilst the rest of the class worked on their class work, and Mrs Chadbourne stared us all down, then brought April over too. My face - and stomach - dropped. I remember knowing instantly that we had been rumbled and feeling SO awful about it. Mrs Chadbourne gave some speech about us needing to look after other peoples feelings more, and whilst everyone else seemed to be staring daggers at Roxanne (who had switched up on us and had been the person to rat us out), I was looking at April's devastated face. I burst out crying, apologising manically, and she started crying too saying she forgave me and we both hugged. Mrs Chadbourne commended me on being the first to apologise and sentenced all of us to a lunchtime detention - unheard of in a primary school, seriously who would do that?</p><p>Even though April had forgiven me, I remember spending a really long time after feeling awful every time I looked at her. It didn't help that I apparently looked so wretched that Mrs Chadbourne let me leave the lunchtime detention early because \"I know it wasn't you - that the other girls just dragged you along\". It ALSO didn't help that April's mum was my hairdresser, and we used to go to her house for my appointments. Every time me and my brother got a trim, I had to spend at least half an hour hanging out with April, and I could never quite get past the sinking feeling in my stomach when I hung out with her since.</p><p>I really aim not to hurt people on purpose in my life, for obvious reasons. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. I remember saying exactly one thing that mostly boiled down to: \"I don't like her singing voice in assemblies\" (we went to a Church of England school - hymns were daily and VERY annoying). </p><p>At the end of the break we all went our separate ways back to class, and I felt at least a little comforted by the fact that no one seemed to be bringing up our little bitch-fest after it had concluded.</p><p>Until, terrifyingly, all of our group were called to the front of the class the next day.</p><p>We huddled at the front of the room whilst the rest of the class worked on their class work, and Mrs Chadbourne stared us all down, then brought April over too. I was still in a phase where I thoroughly enjoyed make-believe games, so I didn't join them very often, but they were there from year 5 onwards. </p><p>The event in question happened on one of the days in year 6 that I was spending time with the gynmastics girls instead of my usual make-believe friends. We had all gathered in a little huddle in the playground when one of us had started talking specifically about another girl in our class - April. Suddenly, with an viciousness I didn't really realise people had at the age of 11, the entire group of girls was insulting and laughing at April behind her back. Most shockingly, her supposed 'best friend' Roxanne was leading the charge. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. So I joined in. I remember saying exactly one thing that mostly boiled down to: \"I don't like her singing voice in assemblies\" (we went to a Church of England school - hymns were daily and VERY annoying). </p><p>At the end of the break we all went our separate ways back to class, and I felt at least a little comforted by the fact that no one seemed to be bringing up our little bitch-fest after it had concluded.</p><p>Until, terrifyingly, all of our group were called to the front of the class the next day.</p><p>We huddled at the front of the room whilst the rest of the class worked on their class work, and Mrs Chadbourne stared us all down, then brought April over too. My face - and stomach - dropped. I remember knowing instantly that we had been rumbled and feeling SO awful about it. Mrs Chadbourne gave some speech about us needing to look after other peoples feelings more, and whilst everyone else seemed to be staring daggers at Roxanne (who had switched up on us and had been the person to rat us out), I was looking at April's devastated face. I burst out crying, apologising manically, and she started crying too saying she forgave me and we both hugged. Mrs Chadbourne commended me on being the first to apologise and sentenced all of us to a lunchtime detention - unheard of in a primary school, seriously who would do that?</p><p>Even though April had forgiven me, I remember spending a really long time after feeling awful every time I looked at her. It didn't help that I apparently looked so wretched that Mrs Chadbourne let me leave the lunchtime detention early because \"I know it wasn't you - that the other girls just dragged you along\". It ALSO didn't help that April's mum was my hairdresser, and we used to go to her house for my appointments. Every time me and my brother got a trim, I had to spend at least half an hour hanging out with April, and I could never quite get past the sinking feeling in my stomach when I hung out with her since.</p><p>I really aim not to hurt people on purpose in my life, for obvious reasons. But this might be the one time I remember knowing and fully understanding that I was going to hurt someone's feelings with my actions, and knowing that it was wrong. It was actually a pretty great teaching moment - I did something wrong, and faced almost immediate consequences. When we reached year 5 there started to be little groups forming - groups that would eventually become the 'popular' kids, the nerds, etc. One of these was a group of girls who would go and stand at the back of the playground by a fence and do an 11 year old's best impression of gymnastics (mostly just handstands and cartwheels) and chat. I was still in a phase where I thoroughly enjoyed make-believe games, so I didn't join them very often, but they were there from year 5 onwards. </p><p>The event in question happened on one of the days in year 6 that I was spending time with the gynmastics girls instead of my usual make-believe friends. We had all gathered in a little huddle in the playground when one of us had started talking specifically about another girl in our class - April. Suddenly, with an viciousness I didn't really realise people had at the age of 11, the entire group of girls was insulting and laughing at April behind her back. Most shockingly, her supposed 'best friend' Roxanne was leading the charge. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. So I joined in. I remember saying exactly one thing that mostly boiled down to: \"I don't like her singing voice in assemblies\" (we went to a Church of England school - hymns were daily and VERY annoying). </p><p>At the end of the break we all went our separate ways back to class, and I felt at least a little comforted by the fact that no one seemed to be bringing up our little bitch-fest after it had concluded.</p><p>Until, terrifyingly, all of our group were called to the front of the class the next day.</p><p>We huddled at the front of the room whilst the rest of the class worked on their class work, and Mrs Chadbourne stared us all down, then brought April over too. Mrs Chadbourne gave some speech about us needing to look after other peoples feelings more, and whilst everyone else seemed to be staring daggers at Roxanne (who had switched up on us and had been the person to rat us out), I was looking at April's devastated face. I burst out crying, apologising manically, and she started crying too saying she forgave me and we both hugged. Most shockingly, her supposed 'best friend' Roxanne was leading the charge. I remember at the time feeling very uneasy about the topic of conversation, but it was right at that age where you started to realise you would do just about anything to fit in with people and avoid becoming their next target. So I joined in. I remember saying exactly one thing that mostly boiled down to: \"I don't like her singing voice in assemblies\" (we went to a Church of England school - hymns were daily and VERY annoying). </p><p>At the end of the break we all went our separate ways back to class, and I felt at least a little comforted by the fact that no one seemed to be bringing up our little bitch-fest after it had concluded.</p><p>Until, terrifyingly, all of our group were called to the front of the class the next day.</p><p>We huddled at the front of the room whilst the rest of the class worked on their class work, and Mrs Chadbourne stared us all down, then brought April over too. My face - and stomach - dropped. I remember knowing instantly that we had been rumbled and feeling SO awful about it. Mrs Chadbourne gave some speech about us needing to look after other peoples feelings more, and whilst everyone else seemed to be staring daggers at Roxanne (who had switched up on us and had been the person to rat us out), I was looking at April's devastated face. I burst out crying, apologising manically, and she started crying too saying she forgave me and we both hugged. Mrs Chadbourne commended me on being the first to apologise and sentenced all of us to a lunchtime detention - unheard of in a primary school, seriously who would do that?</p><p>Even though April had forgiven me, I remember spending a really long time after feeling awful every time I looked at her. It didn't help that I apparently looked so wretched that Mrs Chadbourne let me leave the lunchtime detention early because \"I know it wasn't you - that the other girls just dragged you along\". It ALSO didn't help that April's mum was my hairdresser, and we used to go to her house for my appointments. Every time me and my brother got a trim, I had to spend at least half an hour hanging out with April, and I could never quite get past the sinking feeling in my stomach when I hung out with her since.</p><p>I really aim not to hurt people on purpose in my life, for obvious reasons. But this might be the one time I remember knowing and fully understanding that I was going to hurt someone's feelings with my actions, and knowing that it was wrong. It was actually a pretty great teaching moment - I did something wrong, and faced almost immediate consequences. To this day I can remember how guilty and shitty I felt when I realised April had been told everything we said about her, and to be honest that was more than enough of a deterrent to me.
